concepts.def: Hazard is natural threat (volcano); disaster is realised damage to humans; risk depends on exposure and vulnerability.
Stages following disaster: stable, deteriorating, search-rescue, relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction; varies by HIC/LIC.
Hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (Pacific), cyclones (Indian Ocean); form over 27 degrees C ocean; Saffir-Simpson scale 1-5.
Prolonged below-average rainfall; can be meteorological, agricultural or hydrological; East Africa 2011 famine, California 2012-17.
Uncontrolled vegetation fires; intensified by climate change; Australia 2019-20 burnt 18 million hectares, killed 1 billion animals.
Risk = hazard frequency x population x vulnerability; reducing vulnerability through preparation cuts disaster impact.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Challenge of Natural Hazards — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Challenge of Natural Hazards brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Challenge of Natural Hazards.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What ocean temperature is needed for tropical storms?
options: 20 degrees
27 degrees
35 degrees
15 degrees
Beaufort
Richter
Saffir-Simpson
Mercalli

mcqs.q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: The strengthening of the natural greenhouse effect by human activities (mainly burning fossil fuels) which add CO2 and other gases to the atmosphere.
Correlation and causation are the same thing.
The greenhouse effect is entirely man-made and harmful.
It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.

mcqs.q: Why does correlation not imply causation in geographical data?
options: Two variables may correlate because of a third confounding factor, coincidence, or reverse causation — statistical association alone does not prove one causes the other.
MDGs and SDGs are the same — just renamed.
If two variables correlate strongly, one must cause the other.
Correlation and causation are the same thing.

mcqs.q: What changed between the MDGs (Millennium Development Goals) and the SDGs (Sustainable Development Goals)?
options: Correlation and causation are the same thing.
MDGs (2000-2015) targeted LICs on basic poverty/health/education; SDGs (2015-2030) apply to all countries and include environmental and inequality goals — broader, more universal scope.
The SDGs replaced the MDGs because the MDGs were achieved.
MDGs and SDGs are the same — just renamed.
